description: I'm Mohamed from Egypt, a programmer with experience in Python, AI, Next.js, and web development. I work with both traditional coding and AI-assisted development. I'm here to innovate, compete, and win.
summary:
PyroAtlas is a global geospatial platform designed to improve how people explore, interpret, and investigate satellite-based fire observations.
Using NASA's MODIS and VIIRS active-fire datasets as its primary sources, PyroAtlas brings observations from different satellite systems into a harmonized analytical environment. Rather than simply displaying individual hotspots, the platform organizes geographically and temporally related observations into dynamic fire clusters
details: PyroAtlas is our response to the NASA Space Apps challenge on harmonized MODIS and VIIRS hotspot data. We built it on NASA FIRMS (MODIS Collection 6.1 and VIIRS 375 m active-fire detections) and turned those detections into an evidence trail instead of a map of dots. A user selects a region, by drawing on the map or entering coordinates, and a date range. The app shows a burning-activity calendar of monthly detection counts from the early 2000s to the present, using accessible color ramps, an anomaly view against the same month in other years, and a rank against history. The monthly counts can be downloaded as CSV. A daily engine also groups detections into clusters, follows them across days, measures them with deterministic indicators, and selects up to ten for investigation. Each selection stores its parameters, input file hashes and seed, so anyone can reproduce it. We hope this helps early-warning teams, scientists and land managers see fire history and unusual activity quickly, without mistaking a detection for a fire or a count for severity. We built the data pipeline in Python (standard library only), and the web app in JavaScript, HTML and CSS with Leaflet and OpenStreetMap, hosted on GitHub and Vercel. We developed it on my computer, and tested it with Python unittest, Node and Playwright. We used Claude, an AI assistant, to help write and test the code, but no AI is used in the analysis: every result is a deterministic calculation from NASA data, and the data source is acknowledged in the app. The creative part is how the project keeps NASA's data honest. Clusters are ranked by percentile ranks of several indicators, with no invented weights, then chosen by a seeded draw that anyone can reproduce. Labeled reference regions fill the slots when too few clusters qualify, so the app never implies findings that aren't there. If NASA revises its data, the original selection is kept and a revision is added. We respect the differences between the sensors (MODIS 1 km, VIIRS 375 m, different record start dates) and never add them together, we flag near-real-time data as provisional, and we account for the end of Suomi-NPP delivery on 2 Nov 2026. We also considered accessibility (colorblind-safe colors, values in every cell, keyboard use) and storage, keeping only small derived files instead of a copy of NASA's archive. Our thresholds are explicit defaults that still need sensitivity testing with NASA's historical data.
